newsitem.title: CHINA: South China town eyes Hong Kong affluent lifestyle.
newsitem.headline: South China town eyes Hong Kong affluent lifestyle.

text.p: At dusk as light rain falls along the Pearl River, waves of young women, hunched under umbrellas and wearing skin-tight shifts and platform shoes, arrive at a dance hall, riding sidesaddle on the backs of rasping motor scooters.
Dismounting with nervous titters, hand to mouth, the girls straighten their clothes and slink into the hall's dark entrance, which also advertises a kind of acrobatic act as additional entertainment.
"Most of those girls have come from northern China to Humen here in the south to find a better life," explains a man working at the front desk of a hotel across the street.

"There are more ways to make money here than in the north. People work in factories and on building sites. We also have visitors from Hong Kong, where life is lonely. Providing companionship is a business like many others."

Cities and towns along the south China coast live in the shadow of Hong Kong's economic success. Humen, at the mouth of the Pearl River less than two hours from the British territory by ferry, is no exception.
Chinese government officials say the city has only about 60,000 permanent residents but that its population is swollen by two to three times that many ambitious transients.

This is not Shenzen, the special economic zone in southern China where relatively cheap land and labour and investment from just across the border in Hong Kong have created an economic miracle of new factories, office buildings, housing and resort communities.

Humen is on a lower rung of the economic ladder, but it is the same ladder. Fertile fields around the town are yielding to industrial and residential development, attracting yet more labour from the north.

Where signature office towers spike the Hong Kong skyline, the buildings which emerge from the lattice-work of bamboo scaffolding on Humen's proliferating commercial cnnstruction sites tend to be mid-rise and comparatively modest in design.

Hong Kong has upscale shopping malls bulging with designer baubles while Humen boasts a frenetic covered market jammed with succulent fruits and vegetables and streets lined with deep, dingy storefronts offering single lines of goods.
A shop selling nothing but rows of hospital green sewing machines stands cheek-by-jowl with one stocking only clocks and another displaying dusty bolts of cloth.

There is no need in Humen for Hong Kong's fancy packaging and marketing skills. This is not a city where people who have everything must be coaxed to buy more. Bicycles and motor scooters clog its streets, not Mercedes and Rolls Royces.
And yet the same race for riches that animates Hong Kong obviously powers Humen.
The middle-class Chinese men who pack a riverfront restaurant for dim sum (snacks) on Sunday morning wear electronic pagers on their belts and carry mobile phones which bleep throughout breakfast.

Their wives ostentatiously display gold jewelerlry, ignoring spoiled children who race between tables practising Kung Fu kicks and sword thrusts with umbrellas, a scene that could easily be set in Hong Kong.

There's an attractive compound of new, luxury low-rise flats in the centre of town, some owned by locals and others by people from Hong Kong who bought them as inexpensive second homes. The development is so well done it would not look out of place in California.
What Humen lacks in Hong Kong glitz it makes up for in human scale and pace. Sampans rock gently in the shadows along the river, their charcoal braziers trailing acrid smoke into the night.

A gaggle of sassy women stand laughing under fluorescent light in front of a beauty parlour, known to offer other services, while its proprietor sprawls in an easy chair on the pavement, picking his teeth.
Humen's moment in history came in 1839 when China seized 20,000 chests of British opium and destroyed them on the town's waterfront.
The incident sparked the first Opium War and led to Britain's seizure of a barren island known as Hong Kong.

Now the glittering prize of Hong Kong is set to revert to Chinese control at midnight on June 30 and the historical divide which separated these two Chinese cities for more than 150 years seems likely to close quickly.

"Humen is a good city, a good place to work," explained Shai Ji An, a 22-year old mechanic in Humen. "Everyone in China wants to come to Guandong (province) and Humen because we have plenty of jobs and there are lots of things to buy."
